claims.text: The starting high-entropy alloy is a metallic phase with a largely random elemental distribution and inherent chemical disorder at ambient conditions.
Moderate local chemical inhomogeneities induce lattice distortions in the alloy.
The induced lattice distortions enhance electron–phonon coupling.
Regions with enhanced electron–phonon coupling can connect into a percolative network.
Formation of the percolative network enables Cooper pairing and superconductivity at low temperature.
Controlled annealing can modify local chemical order and lattice distortions without fully eliminating the alloy's chemical disorder.
Controlled increases in local chemical order induce local lattice strains.
An optimal degree of local ordering and associated distortion produces a stronger superconducting signature than the as-synthesized baseline.
Optimally ordered samples will have a higher superconducting critical temperature than the as-synthesized baseline.
The as-synthesized, fully disordered alloy is expected to exhibit little or no superconductivity under the same low-temperature conditions.
The proposed behavior requires the alloy to retain significant chemical disorder and localized lattice distortions.
Excessive ordering may remove the disorder-related effect and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Transformation to an amorphous phase may invalidate the hypothesis because the conduction mechanism would be fundamentally different.
